title: Networking Fundamentals
summary: What networks are, why they exist, and the key terms — packets, bandwidth, latency — every engineer must know.

blocks.markdown:
A **computer network** is two or more computers linked so they can exchange data.

- Without networks every file transfer would require a physical drive.
- Networks unlock **shared resources** (files, printers, internet access) and **communication** (email, video calls).
- Everything you do online rides a network — browsers, apps, APIs, cloud services.
- Understanding networks is foundational to backend, infra, and security work.

blocks.subTitle: The scope ladder
blocks.markdown:
Networks are classified by how far they reach.

| Type | Scope | Example |
|---|---|---|
| LAN | One building / campus | Office Wi-Fi |
| MAN | A city | Metro fibre ring |
| WAN | Countries / continents | The Internet |

Most day-to-day engineering sits at the LAN and WAN boundary.

blocks.subTitle: LAN
blocks.markdown:
A **LAN (Local Area Network)** connects devices in a small area — a home, an office floor, a campus building.

- Typically fast (100 Mbps – 10 Gbps) and low-latency.
- Owned and managed by one organisation.
- Your laptop talking to your home router is a LAN.

See [network-devices](network-devices) for the hardware that builds a LAN.

blocks.subTitle: WAN & MAN
blocks.markdown:
A **WAN (Wide Area Network)** spans cities, countries, or the globe by leasing long-distance links from telcos.

- Slower and higher-latency than a LAN — the signal travels farther.
- No single owner; agreements between providers stitch it together.
- The **Internet** is the largest WAN.

A **MAN (Metropolitan Area Network)** sits between the two — city-scale fibre connecting offices or campuses.

blocks.subTitle: Client-server
blocks.markdown:
In **client-server** architecture one machine (the **server**) holds resources and one or many **clients** request them.

- The server is always on and reachable at a known address.
- Clients initiate requests; the server responds.
- Most of the web works this way: your browser (client) fetches a page from a web server.

Centralised control makes management and security straightforward.

blocks.subTitle: Peer-to-peer
blocks.markdown:
In **peer-to-peer (P2P)** every node is both client and server — any machine can request or provide resources.

- No central server to fail or bottleneck.
- Scales well for sharing (BitTorrent), but harder to secure and manage.
- Each node shares the load: the more peers, the more total capacity.

Trade-off vs. client-server: resilience and scale vs. control and simplicity.

blocks.subTitle: Packets
blocks.markdown:
Networks don't send a whole file in one lump. They split data into small chunks called **packets**.

- Each packet has a **header** (source, destination, sequence number) and a **payload** (the data).
- Packets can take different routes and arrive out of order — the receiver reassembles them.
- Splitting lets many conversations share the same link without one hogging it.

See [osi-tcpip-models](osi-tcpip-models) for how packets are wrapped at each layer.

blocks.subTitle: Bandwidth
blocks.markdown:
**Bandwidth** is the maximum amount of data a link can carry per second — the pipe's width.

- Measured in bits per second: Mbps, Gbps.
- A 100 Mbps link can push at most 100 million bits every second under ideal conditions.
- Bandwidth is a **capacity** figure, not a speed figure — a wide pipe doesn't mean fast delivery.

blocks.subTitle: Latency & throughput
blocks.markdown:
Two more essential terms.

- **Latency** — the time for one packet to travel from sender to receiver. Measured in milliseconds. Also called **RTT** (round-trip time) when measured both ways.
- **Throughput** — the actual data delivered per second in practice, after accounting for congestion, retransmits, and overhead. Always ≤ bandwidth.

High bandwidth with high latency still feels slow. Low latency matters most for interactive work (gaming, video calls); throughput matters for bulk transfers (backups, streaming).

They are not the same thing.

- **The Internet** is the global network infrastructure — billions of devices linked by routers and cables. It carries all traffic: email, video calls, file transfers, the Web.
- **The Web** is one service that runs on top of the Internet — webpages linked by URLs and fetched with HTTP.

Analogy: the Internet is the roads; the Web is one type of vehicle (a car) that uses them. Email and SSH are other vehicles on the same roads.

blocks.subTitle: Bandwidth vs latency vs throughput
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is the difference between bandwidth, latency, and throughput?**

**Bandwidth** is the link's maximum capacity (pipe width). **Latency** is the time for one packet to reach the destination (pipe length effect). **Throughput** is actual data delivered per second — always less than bandwidth due to real-world overhead.

Think of a highway: bandwidth is lanes, latency is the drive time, throughput is cars actually arriving per hour.

blocks.subTitle: LAN vs WAN
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is the difference between a LAN and a WAN?**

A **LAN** is a private network within one building or campus — fast, low-latency, single-owner. A **WAN** spans cities or countries over leased telco links — slower, higher-latency, multiple owners.

Your office network is a LAN; the Internet connecting your offices globally is a WAN.

blocks.subTitle: Internet vs the Web
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is the difference between the Internet and the Web?**

The **Internet** is the global physical and logical network — the infrastructure. The **Web** is a single application layer service built on top of it: HTML pages linked by URLs, delivered over HTTP.

Other services (email, SSH, DNS, streaming) also run on the Internet — they're not the Web.
